items.summary: The June 11 morning is the most economically complex pre-FOMC window of the Warsh chairmanship cycle to date. The May PPI released this morning — +1.1% MoM versus the +0.7% Dow Jones consensus, placing the 12-month wholesale inflation rate at 6.5% — is the sharpest above-consensus PPI beat of the Hormuz inflation cycle. The wholesale reading compounds the May CPI confirmed June 10 (4.2% YoY at consensus, highest since April 2023, core 2.9% in-line). Taken together, the May CPI-PPI pairing confirms that the Iran-energy inflation shock is fully transmitted through both the consumer and producer price channels — with PPI's above-consensus monthly print suggesting pipeline inflation pressure has not yet peaked despite CPI at-consensus providing short-term headline relief. The PPI miss narrows the interpretive space for Warsh's hawkish-pause framing at the June 16–17 inaugural meeting: a 6.5% annualized wholesale rate five days before the FOMC press conference is difficult to characterize as transitory. Warsh advances to Day 28 of complete silence. CME FedWatch June hike probability remains approximately 3% — the June hold at 3.50–3.75% is the operative consensus. Late-2026 hike probability nudging toward approximately 72%, up from ~70% pre-CPI as the PPI print adds incremental trajectory confirmation. Cleveland PCE nowcast holds at 4.18%. Bond vigilante pressure remains active (30-year Treasury near 5.18% recent high). The June 7 BLS jobs report — non-farm payrolls nearly double analyst expectations — triggered a Nasdaq -4% session and S&P -1.2%; Barclays issued an 'entering the warning zone' note on AI equity multiples citing capex bubble risk concurrent with elevated inflation. US equity markets open the June 11 session carrying the June 7 jobs-shock hangover, the PPI miss, and FIFA Day 1 security premium — but with the DHS/ICE passage providing a modest domestic stability signal. The Brent ~$94 continuing easing trend remains the primary delay-not-collapse confirmation in the commodity channel.

items.summary: Four secondary infrastructure threads entering June 11 morning. First: NSF Newport OR ocean observatory (last remaining PNW floating station after Washington stations removed September 2025) continues advancing toward end-of-June removal — approximately three weeks before structural monitoring loss. The operational window before permanent structural capacity loss narrows daily. Loss of ocean buoy data degrades atmospheric river early detection, marine heat wave and fisheries forecasting, wave height and storm surge coastal emergency management, and Pacific maritime monitoring at precisely the peak summer maritime and wildfire stress period. Second: US grid demand is rising at the fastest pace since World War II, driven primarily by AI data center build-out. The electric utility sector faces unprecedented load growth challenging physical infrastructure and the regulatory structures governing grid development for decades. Global grid investment forecast of approximately $5.8 trillion between 2026–2035 signals the scale of the challenge. DOE's national energy emergency (declared 2025) remains operative — aging plants held online, interconnection queue expediting under emergency authority. Battery storage deployment continues accelerating nationally — 2026 tracking above 2025's record-breaking 10+ GW pace — providing growing grid backstop against drought-reduced PNW hydropower. Interconnection queues remain at historic levels; transmission bottlenecks limit integration velocity. May PPI's +6.5% annualized wholesale print this morning reinforces the cost-of-delay calculus for grid modernization investment. Third: FERC summer assessment confirms PNW drought-reduced hydropower as a specific summer grid vulnerability — BPA output reduction concurrent with above-normal temperature and below-normal precipitation forecast through June. No new emergency grid alerts in the overnight cycle. Fourth: Sound Transit's $34.5B funding gap remains unresolved heading into the June board capital planning session; Link Light Rail is the primary transit mode for Lumen Field FIFA World Cup access — the first Seattle match (Belgium vs Egypt) is T-4 from this morning, and the transit system's structural funding uncertainty is a dependency risk at the precise moment it is most heavily relied upon for mass-event crowd management.

items.summary: Four secondary PNW environmental and civic threads entering June 11 morning. First: PNW fire-drought conditions continue tracking above-normal without overnight ignition. NIFC above-normal Day 11; east Cascades explicitly above normal in June NIFC outlook. May ran +3 to +7°F above normal across Oregon and Washington with 30–50% of normal precipitation; SWE essentially gone at mid-elevations; BPA hydropower output reduced. Oregon wildfire season expected severe and extending into October. Washington snowpack at approximately 50% of normal and melted early. Super El Niño (1-in-4) remains the primary amplifier: higher temperature anomalies, extended season endpoint, increased high-severity fire distribution. Oregon 83% drought (12 counties emergency); Washington drought emergency Day 7 (4th consecutive year). The drought-to-fire transmission timeline is accelerating: east-slope fuel conditions are deteriorating through the pre-ignition drying phase that precedes July's above-normal onset window. Second: NSF Newport OR ocean observatory removal advancing at approximately three weeks from end-of-June target. When removed, the PNW will have zero offshore floating observatories for the first time in decades — degrading atmospheric river early detection, marine heat wave forecasting, and wave height and storm surge coastal emergency management at peak summer maritime stress, concurrent with above-normal wildfire conditions and the FIFA mass-event operational footprint. Third: Oregon gray whale washups continue at 21 YTD (Oregon coast), 17 YTD (Washington) — above the expected annual pace; most carcasses show serious emaciation consistent with Pacific prey availability collapse. Marine ecosystem stress runs concurrent with the ocean monitoring network dismantlement. Fourth: Portland-area weather remains temperate this week (high 60s to low 70s), providing west-slope wildfire fuel moisture reprieve through the first FIFA match weekend (June 15). No heat advisory before late June. East-slope conditions continue deteriorating without the west-slope reprieve.

analyst_summary: June 11, 2026 morning opens at Vibe 3 lower edge — consistent with June 10 evening close. Three structural pillars sustaining Vibe 3 above 2 remain intact through the overnight cycle.
